stem: An insulin-treated adult has an uncertain diabetes classification, and the clinician orders a serum C-peptide level. What information can this test contribute?

options.A: It measures average blood glucose over roughly three months and therefore replaces hemoglobin A1c testing.
options.B: It can help assess residual endogenous insulin secretory reserve and must be interpreted with the clinical context and other diagnostic information.
options.C: It determines diabetes type by itself regardless of insulin therapy, clinical history, renal function, or other diagnostic information.
options.D: It measures renal filtration without providing clinically useful information about endogenous pancreatic insulin secretion.

rationale: Mayo Clinic Laboratories lists serum C-peptide testing as useful for assessing residual endogenous insulin secretory reserve in selected diabetic patients, including those receiving insulin therapy. C-peptide generally parallels endogenous insulin secretion, but kidney failure and other factors can alter levels and Mayo cautions that interpretation must account for clinical context and assay limitations. B is correct; the test is not an HbA1c substitute and does not classify diabetes by itself.
educational_objective: Use C-peptide as supportive information about residual endogenous insulin secretion in selected insulin-treated patients while integrating clinical history and other diagnostic data.
source_version_date: Current Mayo Clinic Laboratories test catalog; live-rechecked August 16, 2026
source_locator: Useful For: assessing insulin secretory reserve in selected diabetic patients receiving insulin therapy, including residual endogenous insulin secretory reserve. Clinical & Interpretive/Cautions: C-peptide reflects endogenous insulin-related changes, is mainly removed by kidneys, and assay/clinical factors affect interpretation.
source_claim_supported: Serum C-peptide can help assess residual endogenous insulin secretory reserve in selected insulin-treated diabetic patients, but results require clinical-context interpretation and do not independently determine diabetes type.

source_original.stem: An insulin-treated adult has an uncertain diabetes classification, and the clinician orders a serum C-peptide level. What information can this test contribute?

options.A: It measures average blood glucose over roughly three months and therefore replaces hemoglobin A1c testing.
options.B: It helps assess endogenous insulin secretion or residual beta-cell secretory reserve and must be interpreted in the clinical context.
options.C: It determines diabetes type by itself regardless of insulin therapy, clinical history, or other diagnostic information.
options.D: It measures renal filtration without providing clinically useful information about endogenous pancreatic insulin secretion.

source_original.rationale: C-peptide is secreted with endogenous insulin and can be used to assess residual endogenous insulin secretory reserve in selected insulin-treated patients. It is not an HbA1c substitute and does not classify diabetes by itself.

correction_summary: Retained key B, made residual endogenous insulin secretory reserve the precise Mayo-supported use, added renal/clinical-context limitations to prevent overclassification, and reduced difficulty from hard to medium.

audit_findings.source_authority: Mayo Clinic Laboratories current test catalog; NCSBN 2026 Test Plan
audit_findings.exact_locator: Mayo CPR Useful For, Clinical & Interpretive, and Cautions; NCSBN Reduction p.13 screenshot verified
audit_findings.claim_audit: Final item correctly limits C-peptide to supportive assessment of endogenous secretory reserve and prevents it from being treated as a stand-alone diabetes classifier or HbA1c replacement.

distractor_audit.A: Incorrect because C-peptide does not measure average three-month glycemia and does not replace HbA1c.
distractor_audit.C: Incorrect because diabetes classification requires clinical and other diagnostic context; renal function and insulin therapy can affect interpretation.
distractor_audit.D: Incorrect because C-peptide provides information about endogenous insulin secretion even though renal clearance affects its concentration.

audit_findings.ambiguity_second_answer: Only B accurately states the test's contribution and necessary interpretive limitations.
audit_findings.cueing: All alternatives describe possible laboratory roles for C-peptide.
audit_findings.blueprint: Reduction of Risk Potential — diagnostic-test interpretation.
audit_findings.independent_second_pass: Re-read current Mayo CPR Useful For/Interpretation/Cautions and NCSBN p.13, then all choices, rationale and renal-context caveat. B remained uniquely correct.
